question: In Shreyas Doshi’s discussion of product decisions, what does he mean when he says a decision can be a “one-way door” for a PM leader?
expected_points: A decision that seems reversible may effectively be irreversible for a PM leader.
Making it can commit the team to ongoing work and add to its workload.
evidence_quote: most doors that look like two-way doors are actually one-way doors. They are two-way doors at Bezos' level, but as a PM leader, for you, they are a one-way door

answer.summary: Doshi warns that a feature may be called a reversible “two-way door,” but a PM leader should not assume it is easy to undo: committing, building, launching, and reporting on it create practical commitment. [S1, S2]

sections.heading: What he means by a “one-way door”
sections.content: A one-way door is a decision you cannot readily come back from. In Doshi’s example, teams treated a feature choice as a quick, reversible two-way-door decision, but once they committed, implementation took five or six weeks and ramping it up took a couple more. By the time it was live and included in a quarterly business review, reversing course was not as simple as “killing” the feature. [S2, S4]

sections.heading: Why PM leaders should be careful
sections.content: Doshi says teams can make these decisions based on whether engineering capacity is available, without clearly evaluating customer motivation, differentiation, or distribution. His point is that calling a decision reversible does not make its real-world consequences reversible; leaders should think through the product rationale before committing. [S1, S2]

sections.heading: What makes it a one-way door in practice
sections.content: Shreyas describes teams assuming they can simply kill a feature later. But after committing, the work may take five or six weeks to build and additional weeks to ramp up. By the time it is out, the team may be preparing to review what it shipped in a quarterly business review. His point is that the decision is not as easy to undo in practice as the “two-way door” label suggests—not that reversal is literally impossible.

sections.content: Before deciding to build, Shreyas says to think clearly about customer motivation, differentiation, and the feature’s distribution approach. He contrasts that with decisions made mainly around whether an engineer is free and when they can work on it.

sections.heading: What makes it a one-way door
sections.content: Shreyas describes teams treating a feature as a quick two-way-door decision because they assume they can simply kill it later. In practice, building it can take five or six weeks, followed by more time to ramp it up; then the team may need to present its performance in a quarterly business review. That commitment can make reversing course much harder than the original “we can undo it” framing suggests. He also warns against deciding mainly based on when an engineer is available: teams should think clearly about customer motivation, differentiation, and distribution before committing.
